To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HLA-DR and DQB alleles and haplotypic combinations are associated with heterosexual transmission of human immunodeficiency type 1 (HIV-1) in Zambian serodiscordant couples.
HLA class II alleles are associated with heterosexual transmission of human immunodeficiency type 1 (HIV-1) in a cohort of initially serodiscordant couples in Zambia.
HLA-DR and -DQ alleles and haplotypic associations are found with heterosexual transmission of human immunodeficiency type 1 in a Zambian cohort.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of HLA class I and II polymorphisms on HIV transmission and disease outcome, and with the genetic basis of HIV-1 diversity in Africa.
the influence of host factors in the heterosexual transmission of HIV-2 and HIV-1 in a population with high prevalence of both viruses.
the genetic and immunological basis of HIV transmission and progression to AIDS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DRB1-DQB1 alleles and/or haplotypes are involved in both transmission and acquisition of HIV-1, although the precise nature of their influence remains unclear.
the genetic associations with heterosexual transmission are not robust and are not consistent across studies.

DRB1*03-DQB1*02 is associated with accelerated HIV seroconversion, DRB1-DQB1 haplotype DRB1*13-DQB1*06 with delayed transmission of HIV, and DRB1-DQ haplotype DR*15-DQ*06 with both seroconversion and transmission of HIV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DRB1-DQB1 haplotypes that are associated with accelerated transmission of HIV- 1 are also associated with accelerated acquisition of infection.

HLA class II alleles and haplotypic associations with HIV-1 infection and heterosexual transmission of the virus in Zambian populations are not as readily apparent as they are for other loci, and that the effects reported here for HLA class II are not as readily interpretative as are those for other loci.
HLA-DR/DQ variants influence heterosexual transmission of HIV- 1, and that this is mediated by the host's immune response to the virus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HLA class II genes are not the major genetic determinants of heterosexual HIV-1 transmission.
the HLA-DR-DQ system does not have a major impact on heterosexual transmission of HIV- 1 in Zambian populations.
HLA class II alleles and haplotypic associations with heterosexual transmission are more complex than originally assumed.
